criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and settlement-level water supply, sewerage, on-site sanitation, and stormwater drainage service access in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, both citywide and across three case-study areas (Kariakoo, Tambukareli, and Kigamboni).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2, but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the paper examines institutional and urban-governance factors affecting water and sanitation provision—specifically institutional fragmentation across ministries, municipal councils, DAWASA, DAWASCO, and EWURA; lack of inter-agency coordination in upgrading project site selection (CIUP vs. DAWASA); and capital-investment prioritization of affluent or master-planned areas (Kariakoo, Kigamboni New City). Under the 2026-10-13 clarification, however, the paper does not examine a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariff or cost-recovery rules, enforcement, discretion, or utility regulatory/ownership rules governing access); instead, it focuses on urban spatial planning, urban growth morphology, infrastructure project delivery/prioritization, and macro-governance fragmentation.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative comparative urban case study based on a year of fieldwork in Dar es Salaam combining citywide and site-specific field surveys, institutional and secondary reports, and interviews with institutional stakeholders and citizens across three selected settlements.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports descriptive service availability and access outcomes at the city and settlement levels, including piped sewerage connection rates, piped water coverage and intermittency, reliance on private wells/kiosks/vendors and on-site pit latrines or septic tanks, and stormwater drainage coverage.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the study setting and settlement populations (Dar es Salaam citywide and three case-study areas: Kariakoo, Tambukareli sub-ward with ~10,000 residents, and Kigamboni with 82,808 residents; interview sample sizes are not reported), qualitative comparative case-study design, urban growth/planning and project-coordination exposures (though not an eligible rule-type mechanism under Criterion 2), and settlement-level infrastructure access outcomes.

evidence_quotes.quote: In 2010, 23,873 households were connected to the sewerage system, meaning that only 3.7 per cent of the city’s households use the piped system.

This paper is the result of a year of research in Dar es Salaam. Research activity was divided into field surveys focused on the entire city, and then on specific surveys within selected case study areas. Data were collected from different institutions, such as municipalities and utilities, as well as from interviews with both stakeholders and citizens.

During the survey, representatives of municipalities, private institutions, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), community-based organizations (CBOs), EWURA, and the Drilling and Dam Construction Agency (DDCA, under the Ministry of Water) all concurred that there is considerable fragmentation in the overall organization of planning, implementation, fund allocations, revenue collection and management of the facilities, and overlapping responsibilities, with implications for the improvement of water and sanitation services.

In contrast to storm drainage, water and sanitation remain left with a total lack of coordination between the different authorities. In fact, CIUP should provide water and sanitation through a memorandum of understanding signed with DAWASA.
The site does not have a piped sewerage system; only 5 per cent of households have septic tanks, which means that out of 10,000 people, 9,500 are using on-site sanitation systems.

raw_response.exposure: Urban growth patterns (vertical densification, informal settlement growth, and master-planned peripheral expansion), spatial planning, infrastructure upgrading project prioritization (DWSSP, CIUP, Kigamboni New City Masterplan), and macro-institutional fragmentation across municipal and water authorities (no rule-type legal/administrative access mechanism studied).
raw_response.outcome: Settlement- and city-level water supply, sewerage, on-site sanitation, and stormwater drainage infrastructure coverage and service availability.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Dar es Salaam, Tanzania (city population 4,364,541 in 2012) and three purposively selected settlement case-study areas: Kariakoo (city centre), Tambukareli sub-ward in Azimio ward (~10,000 residents), and Kigamboni in Temeke Municipality (82,808 residents / 13,883 households); stakeholder and citizen interview sample sizes not reported.
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope clarification. While this qualitative comparative case study examines urban water, sanitation, and drainage conditions in Dar es Salaam and discusses broad institutional fragmentation, lack of municipal-utility coordination in infrastructure upgrading projects (CIUP vs. DAWASA), and investment prioritization across urban settlement types, it focuses on urban spatial planning, settlement morphology, project delivery, and macro-governance background rather than any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, tariff rules, administrative burdens, enforcement, or utility regulatory rules). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would have been included.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative comparative case study (three urban settlement case studies combining field surveys, stakeholder and citizen interviews, and secondary institutional reports)
